caption:
Close your eyes to remember more. Mind goes blank when someone asks what you saw? Shut your eyes, then answer.

WHY: your eyes keep pulling in new things to look at, like a phone lighting up or someone walking past. Shutting them takes that load off, so more of your attention goes into remembering, and it's easier to picture the scene again.

HOW:
1. When someone asks about something you saw or heard, close your eyes before you answer.
2. Keep them shut while you talk it through. Picture where you were standing.
3. Open them when you're done.

THE RESEARCH: in 5 experiments, people watched a short video or a staged live event, then answered questions about it with their eyes open or shut. In 4 of the 5, the eyes-shut group recalled more correct details, without more wrong ones.

THE CATCH: it helps you get back what you saw and heard. It can't add anything you never noticed, and it was tested on recent events, not on things you studied weeks ago.

Do this: Close your eyes, then answer.

Send this to the friend who always says "I don't remember."
Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#focus #memory #studytips #productivity #brainhacks

Sources (checked Oct 27 2026):
1) Perfect, T. J., Wagstaff, G. F., Moore, D., Andrews, B., Cleveland, V., Newcombe, S., Brisbane, K.-A. & Brown, L. (2008). How can we help witnesses to remember more? It's an (eyes) open and shut case. Law and Human Behavior, 32(4), 314–324. doi:10.1007/s10979-007-9109-5. Five experiments (video and staged live events): eyes-closed recall had more correct details in Experiments 1, 3, 4 and 5 (+20% to +74%) with no rise in errors; Experiment 2 showed no overall gain. Checked on the authors' summary in The Jury Expert 20(2), 2008 (thejuryexpert.com) and the PubPeer record of the paper.
2) Vredeveldt, A., Hitch, G. J. & Baddeley, A. D. (2011). Eyeclosure helps memory by reducing cognitive load and enhancing visualisation. Memory & Cognition, 39, 1253–1263. doi:10.3758/s13421-011-0098-8. 80 witnesses: recall was best with eyes closed or a blank screen, worst with distraction: the 'less to look at, more room to remember' line. Checked on the publisher page.
3) Vredeveldt & Penrod (2012), Psychology, Crime & Law: the effect held for a staged street event, 96 students (BPS Research Digest summary).

caption:
Fewer temptations beat more willpower. Move one temptation out of the room.

WHY: every time a temptation is in front of you, you have to say no to it again, and that wears you down. Take it away and there's nothing left to say no to.

HOW:
1. Before you start, look around: what keeps pulling you away? Snacks, the game controller, the TV remote.
2. Pick one.
3. Put it in another room, or a closed drawer, until you're done.

THE RESEARCH: researchers followed 159 first-year university students through a semester. Five times a day for a week, students said what they wanted in that moment and whether they resisted it. At the end of term they rated progress on their goals. Students who ran into more temptations made less progress and felt more drained. How hard they resisted didn't predict their progress at all.

THE CATCH: it's one study and it shows a link, not proof that removing things causes success. Resisting was measured with a single question.

Do this: Move one temptation out of the room.

Send this to the friend who says they just need more willpower.
Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#selfcontrol #focus #habits #productivity #studytips

Source (checked Oct 27 2026 on the authors' PDF, Carleton University Goal Lab):
Milyavskaya, M. & Inzlicht, M. (2017). What's so great about self-control? Examining the importance of effortful self-control and temptation in predicting real-life depletion and goal attainment. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 8(6), 603–611. doi:10.1177/1948550616679237. 159 first-year McGill students; experience sampling 5 times a day for 7 days plus nightly diaries; 107 reported end-of-semester progress on 399 goals. Experiencing temptation predicted less goal progress and more depletion; effortful self-control did not predict goal attainment (Bayesian analyses favoured no effect). Limits: correlational; self-control measured with a single item.
Cut while researching: Ariely & Wertenbroch (2002) 'spaced deadlines' was considered and dropped: a 2026 Psychological Science replication (Hyndman & Bisin) did not reproduce it and Data Colada (post 138) reported data anomalies.
